opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's great to be here.

When we founded AIR, the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua, back in 2020, I spent a lot of time thinking about what kind of institute we wanted to be. Tsinghua already has world-class departments doing fundamental research, and industry has enormous engineering capacity. So the question was: where is the gap, and where can we uniquely add value?

I usually describe our priorities in three ways.

First, we focus on problems that matter to industry and society, not just papers. Our mission is to use AI to solve real problems, real-world problems at scale. That's why the "I" in AIR is "industry." We want our research to have impact, to be deployed, to change how things work in transportation, healthcare, and sustainability.

Second, we chose a few areas rather than trying to do everything. I like to think of it as three major directions. One is robotics and autonomous driving, what I'd call AI for the physical world, intelligent transportation and vehicle-road coordination. The second is smart healthcare and life sciences, AI for biology, drug discovery, computational medicine, where I believe AI will be most transformative over the next decade or two. The third is the Internet of Things and green computing, AI at the edge, efficient models, and how AI can help with carbon and energy. Underneath all of that, of course, are foundation models and generative AI, which have become a common layer across everything we do.

Third, and this is about culture: we try to combine the rigor of academia with the speed and pragmatism of industry. Many of our people, myself included, spent long careers at companies like Microsoft and Baidu. So we work closely with companies, we open-source a lot, we build real systems and test them on real roads and in real hospitals. And we place great emphasis on training young people, students who can move between research and entrepreneurship.

I often summarize it in a simple phrase: we want to do things that are "important, hard, and useful." If it's not important, why do it? If it's not hard, industry can do it on its own. And if it's not useful, it stays in the lab. The intersection of those three is where AIR wants to be.

r001.rationale: The response frames AIR’s mission around solving real-world problems at scale and names broad sectors such as transportation, healthcare, and sustainability, describing work with companies generally rather than service to one company.

fable-5.1.text:
When we set up AIR at Tsinghua in 2020, I had a very simple framing in my mind. I didn't want to build another lab that writes papers and stops there, and I didn't want to build a company either. Tsinghua already has excellent departments doing fundamental research, and China has plenty of companies doing product. The gap, as I saw it, was in between: the place where a technology is mature enough to matter but not yet mature enough to be a business. That's where we live.

So the first priority is choosing the right problems. We picked three directions early on, and we've stayed disciplined about them. One is intelligent transportation, especially autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination. One is AI for healthcare and life science, including drug discovery. And the third is what we call green computing, meaning using AI to make the digital infrastructure itself more efficient, and later this expanded into the broader question of large models and embodied intelligence. The common thread is that each of these is a big, real-world problem where the AI is not the whole answer but is the key that unlocks it. I tell our researchers that if the problem would still be interesting in ten years, it's probably the right problem.

The second priority is people. I spent many years at Microsoft Research and at Baidu, and the lesson I took from both is that institutions don't produce breakthroughs, individuals do, and the institution's job is to protect them. So we recruit people who are world class in their field and then give them freedom and long time horizons. We don't evaluate on paper counts. We ask whether the work changed something, whether it was a system, a dataset, an open source release, or a startup.

And that leads to the third priority, which is industry collaboration done properly. The word "industry" is in our name on purpose. We work very closely with companies, but on our own terms. We don't do contract engineering. We co-define problems, we share talent, and we expect that some of what we build will leave the building. Several teams from AIR have spun out, and I consider that a success, not a loss. A research institute that never loses people to industry is probably not doing anything industry cares about.

If I had to compress all of it: pick long-horizon problems with real-world weight, hire people better than yourself, and keep one foot firmly in academia and one in industry without falling over. That balance is harder than it sounds, and honestly I think maintaining it is the main job.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes working closely with companies, co-defining problems, and spinning out teams, presenting AIR as serving industry broadly rather than one company.

astra-6.text:
I would define our priorities around connecting AI research with real industrial needs. For a university institute, the first responsibility is to do rigorous research and develop new ideas. But we also want those ideas to work outside the laboratory, where the data are imperfect, the constraints are real, and reliability matters.

That means bringing researchers and industry partners together around meaningful problems, then using what we learn from deployment to inform the next round of research. Talent development is central to that process: we want people who understand both the underlying science and the systems needed to put it into practice.

Ultimately, I think we should judge our work by the quality of the research, the people we train, and the value we create for society.

r001.rationale: The response frames the institute around broad industrial needs and collaboration with industry partners, rather than work for one company.

sol-6.1.text: I would define our priorities around connecting AI research with real industrial needs. That means advancing the underlying technology, understanding where it can make a meaningful difference, and working with industry to turn research into practical solutions. Education is also central: we want to develop people who understand both AI and the domains in which it will be used. Across all of that, we need to think about safety and the broader impact of the technology.

r001.rationale: The response describes connecting AI research with real industrial needs and working with industry generally, rather than serving a single company.
